_how_to_use: Fill in `canonical` BEFORE translating anything. One term, one rendering, for the whole language.
verify.py enforces it: if a source field mentions the term on the left, the translation must contain the value on the right.
Leave a value empty to switch that check off.
`watch_variants` is for spellings that drifted in a previous language. Add any you catch; verify.py reports when more than one is used.
`overrides` switches the canonical-term check off for one field, when the ENGLISH source is itself wrong. Give a reason.

overrides.categories.name.2: English says "Dua's Excellence", but this category holds Tasbeeh/Tahmid/Tahlil/Takbeer, and the Bengali says dhikr. Translated as dhikr.
overrides.duas.translation.285: English asks for a successor among the deceased's descendants. The supplied Arabic واخلفه في عقبه and Bengali ask Allah to take care of those left behind; Urdu follows that meaning without repeating the Bengali's duplicated grave supplication.
overrides.duas.translation.294: English adds '(of faith)' to the reward. The supplied Arabic أجره refers to the deceased, as the Bengali also indicates; Urdu preserves that reference without the unsupported English parenthesis.
overrides.duas.translation.295: English renders وعافه as 'give him strength'. The supplied Arabic and Bengali ask for well-being or safety; Urdu uses عافیت عطا فرما.
overrides.duas.translation.297: English calls the deceased the son of a male and female servant. The supplied Arabic عبدك وابن أمتك calls him Allah's servant and the son of His female servant; the Bengali supports this, and Urdu follows it.
overrides.duas.translation.299: As in row 295, Arabic wa aafihaa and Bengali mean well-being, not strength. The stray English masculine pronouns refer to the female deceased; Urdu consistently uses the female context.
overrides.duas.translation.301: English calls her the daughter of male and female servants. Supplied Arabic and Bengali call her Allah's female servant and the daughter of His female servant; Urdu follows those.
overrides.duas.note.310: English asks whether to pray on Laylatul Qadr. Bengali asks what supplication to make, which matches the response teaching a particular dua; Urdu follows Bengali.
overrides.duas.note.315: English adultery is too narrow. Bengali describes sexual conduct, and Bukhari 1894 uses la yarfuth; Urdu preserves the broader meaning. Checked https://sunnah.com/bukhari:1894 .
overrides.duas.translation.316: English describes past actions, but the Arabic and Bengali are a supplication for the hosts; Urdu retains that prayer form.
overrides.duas.name.319: English title mentions only returning, but the main dua and content concern starting a journey and the nested group adds the return wording. Urdu follows the Bengali title covering both.
overrides.duas.translation.321: English safety represents Arabic amanataka; Bengali explicitly says entrusted responsibility. Urdu uses the established religious term amanat.
overrides.duas.note.321: The explanatory rendering repeats the same amanataka phrase as the main translation; Urdu consistently uses amanat rather than English safety. Embedded Latin transliteration remains verbatim.
overrides.duas.name.323: English title says traveller praying for resident, but the actual dua and note concern arriving or stopping at a place. Urdu follows the Bengali subject; retains English #1.
overrides.duas.name.324: English title says traveller praying for resident, but the actual dua and note concern entering a town. Urdu follows the Bengali subject; retains #2.
overrides.duas.content.327: Abu al-Malih is the intermediary narrator, not the Companion who rode behind the Prophet. Use rahimahullah for him and radiyallahu anhu for the unnamed Companion. Checked https://sunnah.com/abudawud:4982 and https://sunnah.com/narrator/4091 .
overrides.duas.note.327: Same narrator attribution and honorific correction as content. Preserve the repeated narration and the note's additional ending.
overrides.duas.translation.329: English capitalizes He Who listens ambiguously. Bengali addresses a hearer, matching Arabic samia samiun; Urdu addresses the listener and does not turn this into a divine name.
overrides.duas.note.331: English says any means of transport, contradicting the boat title and dua. Bengali specifically says land vehicles; Urdu follows that scope while preserving the author's statement.
overrides.duas.content.339: English marks Amr ibn Shuayb as a Companion and vaguely says predecessors. Preserve the chain through his father to his grandfather, use rahimahullah for Amr and radiyallahu anhu for the Companion, and identify preceding prophets as in Bengali and Tirmidhi 3585. Checked https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:3585 .
overrides.duas.note.339: Same chain, honorific and preceding-prophets correction as content; preserve the repeated narration.
overrides.duas.group_items.343.1.note: English incorrectly inserts (the sky) as the subject and says full fair. This is the Prophet staying until daylight brightens, as the parallel narration in row 340 and Bengali show.
overrides.duas.content.347: Both supplied prose versions corrupt the animal and body-part description. The cited Bukhari 5565 explicitly describes two horned black-and-white rams and placing a foot on their sides. Urdu restores those details. Checked https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5565 .
overrides.duas.content.352: Muslim occurs only in the inline citation [Muslim: 780], which the skill requires copying in English. Do not add an Urdu collection name solely to satisfy the canonical-term check.
overrides.duas.note.357: The Uqbah here is Uqbah ibn Muslim, an intermediary narrator in Abu Dawud 466, not the Companion Uqbah ibn Amir. Use rahimahullah rather than the source RA. Checked https://sunnah.com/abudawud:466 .
overrides.duas.content.361: Source Husain (RA) is an attribution error. Hisn al-Muslim attributes these words to Hasan al-Basri; Urdu uses Hasan Basri rahimahullah. Checked https://risala.prh.gov.sa/storage/contents/51/ar_hisnulmuslim.pdf . The frozen Abu Dawood: 441 reference is retained for a separate source audit.
overrides.duas.content.367: Surah occurs only in the inline reference, which is retained verbatim in English per the skill. Do not add an Urdu surah label to the narrative solely for the glossary check.
overrides.duas.note.368: English duplicates the rooster narration in the second paragraph. Bengali and the actual second reference, Abu Dawud 5103, concern dogs and donkeys at night; Urdu follows those, retaining [1] and [2]. Checked https://sunnah.com/abudawud:5103 .
overrides.duas.translation.370: English Messenger is singular, whereas the supplied Arabic rusulihi and Bengali are plural. Urdu correctly says His messengers.
overrides.duas.note.372: Abu Zumayl is the intermediary narrator reporting his question to Ibn Abbas, not a Companion. Urdu uses rahimahullah for him and radiyallahu anhuma for Ibn Abbas. Checked https://sunnah.com/abudawud:5110 .
overrides.duas.translation.379: English repent for me is incorrect for tub alayya, which asks Allah to accept repentance. It also swaps the wrong divine name: supplied Arabic and Bengali replace Rahim with Ghafur while retaining Tawwab.
overrides.duas.note.380: English middle of the night omits the qualifying last part. Bengali and Arabic Tirmidhi 3579 say the last part of the night. The heart wording follows the restrained covering metaphor also used in row 389. Checked https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:3579 .
overrides.duas.content.387: English pray is imprecise: Bengali and the repeated Bukhari 6307 wording ask forgiveness and repent. Urdu explicitly preserves both actions.
overrides.duas.content.388: Arabic Muslim 2702b says al-Agharr was narrating TO Ibn Umar, not quoting FROM him. Abu Burdah is the intermediary narrator, so use rahimahullah. Checked https://sunnah.com/muslim:2702b .
overrides.duas.content.389: English goes astray overstates the meaning. Bengali describes momentary preoccupation; Urdu preserves the covering metaphor of layughanu ala qalbi, matching the parallel narration in row 380. Arabic independently checked at https://sunnah.com/muslim:2702a .
overrides.duas.content.390: English wrongly introduces the displayed text as the prayer tashahhud. The supplied text is Khutbat al-Hajah, as Bengali says. Preserve the initial mention of both teachings but introduce the correct displayed passage.
overrides.duas.translation.390: English omits the kinship clause from Quran 4:1. Supplied Arabic wal-arham and Bengali both include it; Urdu restores it without altering citation numbers.
overrides.duas.translation.394: English and Bengali mistranslate the final clause as gathering or separating good things. Supplied Arabic asks Allah to keep the spouses together in goodness for as long as He joins them, and to separate them in goodness if He separates them.
overrides.duas.translation.412: English omits by Your favour, which is explicit in the supplied Arabic bifadlika and Bengali. Urdu preserves this phrase.
overrides.duas.translation.416: English repeats the grave trial and says wash my sins. Supplied Arabic and Bengali have one grave-trial clause and ask to wash the heart with snow and hail water. Urdu follows those without the English duplication.
overrides.duas.translation.417: English omits Lord of the earth, which appears in the supplied Arabic and Bengali. Restore it in Urdu and render the present grasp of the forelock rather than the English future tense.
overrides.duas.note.365: English reverses the wording of the hypothetical regret. Bengali and Muslim 2664 say if I had done such-and-such, this would have happened. Urdu preserves that conditional form.
overrides.duas.note.381: The prose omits the speaker. Musnad Ahmad 712 explicitly has Ali reporting that the Prophet addressed him; restore that attribution. Retain the unusual already-forgiven wording, which really occurs in the Arabic. Checked the Musnad text reproduced at https://dorar.net/h/JcEng0hJ?osoul=1 .
overrides.duas.content.394: The cited Adab al-Zifaf discusses a raised report but explicitly prefers the version stopping at Ibn Masud. Attribute this instruction to Ibn Masud rather than unconditionally to the Prophet; frozen reference remains unchanged. Checked https://islamhouse.com/read/ar/????-??????-??-?????-???????-276162 , section 2, footnote to the second report.
overrides.duas.note.397: The supplied claim about Companions conflicts with the Hasan al-Basri attribution in row 396 and the Nawawi recommendation for the reply in row 362. Urdu uses the accurate broader attribution to scholars; see Hisn al-Muslim chapter 47, https://risala.prh.gov.sa/storage/contents/51/ar_hisnulmuslim.pdf .
overrides.duas.note.428: English reverses the hypothetical by saying 'if I had not done that'. The supplied Arabic in Muslim 2664 says law anni fa'altu, and Bengali likewise says 'if I had done'; Urdu follows that wording, consistent with row 365. Checked https://sunnah.com/muslim:2664 .
overrides.duas.content.445: English says Allah will forgive the debt. Bengali says He will free the person from debt, which is the intended meaning in this debt-settlement context; Urdu says Allah will grant release from debt.
overrides.duas.translation.451: English paraphrases wallahu hasibuhu as Allah knowing the exact truth. The supplied Arabic literally makes Allah the person's Reckoner; Urdu preserves that meaning.
overrides.duas.group_items.453.1.content: The malformed English changes the addressee and speaker. Muslim 2346 has people asking Abdullah ibn Sarjis whether the Messenger sought forgiveness for him; Abdullah answers yes, for them too, and recites the verse. Urdu restores those speakers. Checked https://sunnah.com/muslim:2346 .
overrides.duas.content.458: English compresses Sa'd's offer into half his family and property. Bukhari 5167 says Sa'd ibn al-Rabi offered half his property and one of his two wives after divorce; Urdu states the actual offer without the misleading half-family wording. Checked https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5167 .
overrides.duas.note.458: English gives two awkward alternatives for the mahr. Bukhari 5167 states gold equal to the weight of a date stone; Urdu uses that exact meaning. Checked https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5167 .
overrides.duas.content.463: English accidentally repeats returning the greeting, creating six rights after announcing five. Bengali and Bukhari 1240 contain exactly five; Urdu removes the duplicate and preserves those five. Checked https://sunnah.com/bukhari:1240 .
overrides.duas.content.469: English is grammatically malformed and makes the listener the possible speaker. Tirmidhi 2741 explicitly instructs the person who sneezes to say this praise; Urdu restores that speaker. Checked https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:2741 .
overrides.duas.content.471: English is grammatically malformed and appears to make the sneezer say yarhamukallah. Tirmidhi 2741 has another person say it to the sneezer, who then gives the displayed reply; Urdu makes the exchange explicit. Checked https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:2741 .
overrides.duas.translation.478: As in row 451, supplied Arabic wallahu hasibuhu makes Allah the person's Reckoner. Urdu preserves that wording instead of the looser English paraphrase.
overrides.duas.translation.483: English mistranslates qurbatan as the reward of a sacrificial slaughter. The supplied Arabic, Bengali and Bukhari 6361 say a means of nearness to Allah; Urdu restores that meaning, consistent with row 450. Checked https://sunnah.com/bukhari:6361 .
overrides.duas.translation.491: English adds Paradise to 'make it a treasure for me'. The supplied Arabic indaka and Bengali say 'with You'; Urdu follows them. Checked https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:3424 .
overrides.duas.content.492: English renders Arabic tiratan mechanically as deprivation descending. Bengali gives regret; Urdu uses the natural hadith sense, 'a cause of regret from Allah', for both sitting and lying. Checked https://sunnah.com/abudawud:4856 .
overrides.duas.translation.494: English says All-Forgiving, but the supplied Arabic ends al-Rahim and Bengali says Merciful. Urdu therefore uses 'Most Merciful' rather than repeating row 474, whose Arabic ends al-Ghafur.
overrides.duas.content.497: The English ending is badly corrupted. Urdu restores the instruction to eat with the right hand and from what is directly in front, followed by Umar ibn Abi Salamah's statement that he continued eating that way. Checked https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5376 .
overrides.duas.name.501: English says the dua is between eating and drinking. Muslim 2734a says Allah is pleased when a servant praises Him after eating food or drinking; Urdu corrects the timing. Checked https://sunnah.com/muslim:2734a .
overrides.duas.content.501: Same timing correction as the title: praise follows eating or drinking, rather than occurring between them. Checked https://sunnah.com/muslim:2734a .
overrides.duas.content.511: English corrupts the opening instruction. Bukhari 3304 says to keep children close when night begins because devils spread, then release them after part of the night has passed; Urdu restores that wording. Checked https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3304 .
overrides.duas.note.512: English has the nonsensical phrase 'donkeys of dogs'. Abu Dawud 5103 says dogs barking and donkeys braying at night; Urdu restores both animals and the reason for seeking refuge. Checked https://sunnah.com/abudawud:5103 .
overrides.duas.translation.513: English omits la ilaha illa anta, which is present in the supplied Arabic and Bengali. Urdu restores 'there is no deity worthy of worship except You'.
overrides.duas.content.516: English calls the wind Allah's 'liveliness'. Abu Dawud 5097 describes wind as being from Allah's mercy; Urdu follows the hadith. Checked https://sunnah.com/abudawud:5097 .
overrides.duas.content.518: English leaves the first-person narrator unnamed. Bukhari 3206 identifies her as Aisha; Urdu names her so the narration and direct address remain clear. Checked https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3206 .
overrides.duas.translation.523: English uses 'pardon us' for wa aafina. The supplied Arabic asks for well-being or safety; Urdu uses عافیت عطا فرما.
overrides.duas.translation.524: English mistranslates the opening as reliance. The supplied Arabic la tayra illa tayruka and Bengali concern omens; Urdu states that no omen has effect apart from Allah's decree.
overrides.duas.note.524: English omits the statement that gives the expiation its context. The supplied Bengali and Musnad Ahmad 7045 state that allowing an omen to stop an intended action is shirk; Urdu restores that sentence before the Companions' question.
overrides.duas.note.531: English labels al-Aswad with RA, but al-Aswad ibn Yazid is the intermediary narrator asking Aisha. Urdu uses rahimahullah for him while retaining radiyallahu anha for Aisha. The chain is visible in https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5741 .
overrides.duas.translation.535: English omits bi-idhni rabbina. The supplied Bengali and Bukhari 5745 include healing by permission of our Lord; Urdu restores that clause. Checked https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5745 .
overrides.duas.group_items.536.0.note: English says Uthman ibn Abi al-As reported an 'explanation' of his body. Muslim 2202 records his complaint of pain; Urdu restores the complaint and the Prophet's instructions. Checked https://sunnah.com/muslim:2202 .
overrides.duas.content.538: English misidentifies the opening transmitters as Abdur Rahman ibn Abi Layla and his father. The cited Tirmidhi 969 has Thuwayr ibn Abi Fakhitah narrating from his father; Urdu follows that chain and the cited report rather than the extra clauses in Bengali. Checked https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:969 .
overrides.duas.content.544: English names only Abu Hurayrah, but Tirmidhi 3430 has al-Agharr Abu Muslim bearing witness from both Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Abu Hurayrah. Urdu restores both Companion narrators. Checked https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:3430 .
overrides.duas.group_items.544.3.note: The malformed English makes Allah the speaker of the concluding promise. Tirmidhi 3430 first gives Allah's affirmation, then attributes 'whoever says it during illness...' to the Prophet. Urdu makes both speakers explicit. Checked https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:3430 .
overrides.duas.content.546: English omits whom to prompt and is grammatically incomplete. Muslim 916a says to prompt those who are dying to recite the declaration of faith; Urdu restores the object. Checked https://sunnah.com/muslim:916a .
overrides.duas.note.4: Surah occurs only in the inline citation, which remains normalized English under the project rules. Do not add an Urdu surah label solely to satisfy the canonical-term check.
overrides.duas.translation.5: English ends with 'You are upon a straight path', but the supplied Arabic and Bengali say that Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path. Urdu follows them.
overrides.duas.translation.9: English renders wa aafini as 'strengthen me'. The supplied Arabic and Bengali ask for well-being; Urdu correctly uses عافیت.
overrides.duas.translation.11: English begins 'O Allah', but the supplied Arabic says Rabbi and Bengali likewise addresses 'my Lord'. Urdu follows the actual invocation: اے میرے رب.
overrides.duas.note.13: English renders dandanah as reciting beautifully. Ibn Majah 910 describes the man's inability to make the Prophet's and Muadh's detailed supplications and the reply that their supplication revolves around seeking Paradise and refuge from Hell; Urdu restores that sense. Checked https://sunnah.com/ibnmajah:910 .
overrides.duas.content.14: English says one day, but the supplied Bengali says after some days and the Arabic of Tirmidhi 3514 has ayyaman. Urdu uses 'after a few days'. Checked https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:3514 .
overrides.duas.group_items.29.0.translation: English omits wa aafini, although it is present in the supplied nested Arabic. Urdu restores the request for well-being.
overrides.duas.content.30: English omits that the new Muslim was first taught the prayer. The supplied Bengali and Muslim 2697b include this before the instruction to supplicate; Urdu restores it. Checked https://sunnah.com/muslim:2697b .
overrides.duas.translation.30: English omits wa aafini, which is present in the supplied Arabic, Bengali and Muslim 2697b. Urdu restores 'grant me well-being'. Checked https://sunnah.com/muslim:2697b .
overrides.duas.name.254: Surah occurs only inside the parenthetical Quran citation. The citation remains in English under the project rules, so no Urdu surah label is added solely for the canonical-term check.
overrides.duas.translation.281: Surah occurs only inside the inline Quran citation. The citation remains in English under the project rules, so no Urdu surah label is added solely for the canonical-term check.
overrides.duas.note.496: Tirmidhi occurs only inside the inline hadith citation. The citation remains in English under the project rules, so no Urdu collection name is added solely for the canonical-term check.
overrides.duas.content.33: English incorrectly gives Ibn Qudamah the Companion honorific RA. He is one of the transmitters whose version specifies the right hand; Urdu uses rahimahullah. Checked the chain at https://sunnah.com/abudawud:1502 .
overrides.duas.content.38: English says 'on the last night', but the cited Tirmidhi narration refers to the latter part of the night. Urdu states the intended time clearly.
overrides.duas.translation.47: English loosely says 'take me out of my plight'. The supplied Arabic ajurni fi musibati asks for reward in the calamity, and wakhluf li khayran minha asks for a better replacement; Urdu preserves both clauses.
overrides.duas.note.49: English mechanically renders the Prophet's question as 'such and such a word'. In context he asks who uttered the displayed words; Urdu makes that referent explicit. Checked https://sunnah.com/muslim:601 .
overrides.duas.content.59: English omits 'and the Prophets before me'. The supplied Bengali and Tirmidhi 3585 both include this clause; Urdu restores it. Checked https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:3585 .
overrides.duas.content.63: English incorrectly begins with Umm Darda as narrator while continuing in Safwan's first person, and labels Safwan RA. The actual chain has Safwan ibn Abdullah narrating his exchange with Umm Darda; Urdu restores the speaker and uses rahimahullah for Safwan. The same chain is visible at https://sunnah.com/adab/31/22 .
overrides.duas.note.65: English labels the sub-narrator Abd al-Malik ibn Umayr with RA. He is a later transmitter, so Urdu uses rahimahullah. The wording about small girls is retained accurately. Checked https://sunnah.com/bukhari:755 .
overrides.duas.content.66: English says the fasting person's supplication is accepted when he breaks his fast, but the supplied Bengali and the Arabic hatta yuftir in Tirmidhi 3598 say until he breaks his fast. Urdu follows the Arabic timing. Checked https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:3598 .
overrides.duas.name.69: English calls this the oppressed person's supplication, but the content is Quran 27:62 about the desperate or distressed person. Urdu follows the actual verse subject.
overrides.duas.translation.73: As in row 47, English omits the explicit request for reward in the calamity. The supplied Arabic and Bengali include it; Urdu restores that meaning.
overrides.duas.name.77: English calls this the excellence of dua, but the report itself concerns sitting with people remembering Allah, and Bengali likewise identifies dhikr. Urdu names the actual subject.
overrides.duas.translation.83: English incorrectly asks for the good of this day. The supplied Arabic says hadhihi al-laylah and the evening context requires night; Urdu follows the Arabic.
overrides.duas.translation.89: English incorrectly says All-Seeing. The supplied Arabic al-Sami and the English note both say All-Hearing; Urdu follows the Arabic.
overrides.duas.name.93: English title says morning and evening, but the instruction and report specify reciting this in the morning. Urdu names the actual time.
overrides.duas.note.100: English confuses Abu Bakrah with Abu Bakr and labels his son as a Companion. Abu Dawud 5090 has Abdur-Rahman ibn Abi Bakrah addressing his father Abu Bakrah; Urdu restores the names and uses rahimahullah for the intermediary. Checked https://sunnah.com/abudawud:5090 .
overrides.duas.note.111: English gives only the kunyah Abu Malik. Sahih Muslim 2697b and its narrator chain identify him as Sa'd ibn Tariq al-Ashja'i narrating from his Companion father Tariq ibn Ashyam; Urdu supplies their names and correct honorifics. Checked https://sunnah.com/muslim:2697b and https://sunnah.com/narrator/3248 .
overrides.duas.note.144: English and Bengali misname Jabir as Jarir, and both add two rak'ahs to the final instruction. Muslim 2262 names Jabir; Tirmidhi 2280 says only to get up and pray. Urdu follows the cited reports. Checked https://sunnah.com/muslim:2262 and https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:2280 .
overrides.duas.translation.189: English inserts a separate 'You are the King of the heavens and the earth' clause that is absent from the supplied Arabic and the Arabic of Bukhari 1120. Urdu follows the Arabic while retaining its explicit sovereignty clause. Checked https://sunnah.com/bukhari:1120 .
overrides.duas.group_items.192.0.translation: English renders nafthihi as the devil's voice. The supplied Arabic and Abu Dawud 764 say his spitting; Urdu corrects that item while preserving the puffing and evil-suggestion clauses. Checked https://sunnah.com/abudawud:764 .
overrides.duas.content.194: English and Bengali name Shqiq and Qatadah. Bukhari 791 names the Successor Zaid ibn Wahb as the first narrator, and Mishkat 885 names the Companion Abu Qatadah in the second report; Urdu restores both names and their honorifics. Checked https://sunnah.com/bukhari:791 and https://sunnah.com/mishkat:885 .
overrides.duas.note.199: English omits that the same supplication was recited in prostration. Bengali and the Arabic of Abu Dawud 873 include it before the Prophet stood and recited Aal Imran; Urdu restores the omitted clause. Checked https://sunnah.com/abudawud:873 .
overrides.duas.name.205: English calls this a dua while in ruku, but the Bengali title and the supplied Arabic place it in qawmah after rising from ruku. Urdu names the actual position.
overrides.duas.name.206: English calls this a dua while in ruku, but the Bengali title and the supplied Arabic place it in qawmah after rising from ruku. Urdu names the actual position.
overrides.duas.name.207: English calls this a dua while in ruku, but the Bengali title, narration and supplied Arabic place it in qawmah after rising from ruku. Urdu names the actual position.
overrides.duas.name.208: English calls this a dua while in ruku, but the Bengali title and the supplied Arabic place it in qawmah after rising from ruku. Urdu names the actual position.
overrides.duas.name.209: English calls this a dua while in ruku, but the Bengali title and narration place it in qawmah after rising from ruku. Urdu names the actual position.
overrides.duas.note.205: English incorrectly says these words are recited in ruku. Bengali correctly places them while standing fully upright after ruku; Urdu follows that qawmah context.
overrides.duas.translation.209: English omits the second blessing phrase represented by Arabic mubarakan alayhi. Bengali retains it; Urdu expresses the doubled blessing naturally.
overrides.duas.name.212: English title mentions only slow prostration, but the narration condemns failing to complete both ruku and sujud. Urdu names both acts.
overrides.duas.content.212: English and Bengali misname Abu Qatadah as Qatadah. Mishkat 885 explicitly attributes the report to the Companion Abu Qatadah; Urdu restores his name. Checked https://sunnah.com/mishkat:885 .
overrides.duas.translation.216: English uses forgiveness for Arabic mu'aafaatika. Urdu preserves the Arabic sense of protection and well-being with aafiyat.
overrides.duas.translation.225: English adds Paradise to 'make it a treasure for me'. The supplied Arabic, Bengali and Tirmidhi 3424 say 'with You'; Urdu follows them. Checked https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:3424 .
overrides.duas.note.235: English skips the link through Ata ibn al-Sa'ib's father and says Ammar directly taught the people. Nasa'i 1305 has Ata narrating from his father, who followed Ammar, asked him and returned with the dua; Urdu restores that sequence. Checked https://sunnah.com/nasai:1305 .
overrides.duas.note.241: English treats dandanah as reciting beautifully. Ibn Majah 910 says the man could not make the Prophet's and Muadh's detailed supplications; the reply says their supplication also revolves around Paradise and refuge from Hell. The frozen Ibn Majah 3846 reference is retained for source-data review. Checked https://sunnah.com/ibnmajah:910 and https://sunnah.com/ibnmajah:3846 .
overrides.duas.content.242: English and Bengali corrupt the narrator's name as Mizan ibn Arda. Nasa'i 1301 names the Companion Mihjan ibn al-Adra; Urdu restores his name. Checked https://sunnah.com/nasai:1301 .
overrides.duas.translation.243: English adds 'alone, without partner', but the supplied Arabic and Nasa'i 1300 omit that clause in this wording. Urdu follows the supplied and cited Arabic. Checked https://sunnah.com/nasai:1300 .
overrides.duas.note.246: English mechanically says 'such and such a word'. In context the Prophet asks who uttered the displayed words; Urdu makes that referent explicit, as in the parallel row 49. Checked https://sunnah.com/muslim:601 .
overrides.duas.translation.258: English begins O Allah, while the supplied Arabic says Rabbi and Bengali likewise addresses my Lord. Urdu follows the actual invocation: اے میرے رب.
overrides.duas.translation.263: English and Bengali add being victorious as a fourth clause. The supplied Arabic and the cited Darimi wording contain only striving, confronting and fighting with Allah's help; Urdu preserves those three clauses.
overrides.duas.translation.265: English renders Arabic an'ishni wajburni as inspire me and make me obedient. The Arabic asks Allah to raise and strengthen the supplicant and mend his deficiencies; Urdu preserves that meaning.
overrides.duas.note.265: English conflates the Abu Umamah and Abu Ayyub variants and shifts between plural narrators and a singular speaker. Urdu gives their shared meaning without inventing a joint first-person quotation. Checked the source variants at https://dorar.net/h/RIzbaxAY?osoul=1 .
overrides.duas.name.269: English and Bengali call this the excellence of dua after Fajr, but Tirmidhi 586 explicitly concerns sitting in dhikr until sunrise. Urdu names dhikr. Checked https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:586 .
overrides.duas.name.270: English and Bengali call this the excellence of dua, but Muslim 670 concerns remaining on the prayer place after Fajr until sunrise. Urdu names that actual subject. Checked https://sunnah.com/muslim:670a .
overrides.duas.content.270: English incorrectly expands al-subh aw al-ghadah into Fajr or Maghrib and labels the Successor Simak as a Companion. Muslim 670a uses two names for the dawn prayer; Urdu retains Fajr only and uses rahimahullah for Simak. Checked https://sunnah.com/muslim:670a .
overrides.duas.group_items.273.2.translation: English glosses nafth as witchcraft. Abu Dawud 775 renders the supplied Arabic nafthihi as the devil's spitting; Urdu follows the cited report. Checked https://sunnah.com/abudawud:775 .
overrides.duas.name.274: English calls this a dua, while the content and Bengali identify the words recited three times after Witr as dhikr. Urdu names it dhikr.
overrides.duas.name.275: English title says after Witr, but the content says at its end and the note explicitly says the report does not establish whether this was before or after salam. Urdu avoids deciding that ambiguity and says at the end of Witr.
overrides.duas.name.276: This wording continues the after-Witr dhikr in row 274, as the Bengali title also states. Urdu names it dhikr rather than the English title's dua.
overrides.duas.translation.283: English omits the instruction to name the intended matter. The supplied Arabic parenthesis, Bengali context and Bukhari 6382 include that instruction; Urdu restores it. Checked https://sunnah.com/bukhari:6382 .
overrides.duas.translation.318: The supplied Arabic and Bengali insert a bracketed la ilaha illa anta, but the cited Tirmidhi 3446 wording does not contain it and English omits it. Urdu follows the cited primary wording while the frozen supplied Arabic remains unchanged. Checked https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:3446 .
overrides.duas.name.311: English calls this a dua, but the content expressly says there is no masnun opening dua and instead explains intention. Urdu accurately names the subject as the intention for beginning the fast.
overrides.duas.note.320: English and Bengali reverse the direction by saying the traveller should address the person seeing him off. Ibn Majah 2825 has the Prophet say these words while seeing Abu Hurayrah off; Urdu corrects that direction while retaining the broader statement that either person may pray for the other. Checked https://sunnah.com/ibnmajah:2825 .
overrides.duas.translation.324: English uses singular 'I seek refuge' in the final clause, but the supplied Arabic has plural na'udhu and Bengali also uses plural. Urdu follows those with 'we seek refuge' while retaining the singular opening request.
overrides.duas.translation.355: English and Bengali render nafthihi as witchcraft or magic. The supplied Arabic and cited Abu Dawud 775 render it as the devil's spitting; Urdu follows the cited wording, consistent with the parallel wording in row 273. Checked https://sunnah.com/abudawud:775 .
overrides.duas.translation.411: The supplied Arabic starts halfway through Quran 14:37 and omits the opening settlement clause, while English translates the complete cited verse. The primary Quran text includes that opening, so Urdu retains the complete verse meaning; the frozen supplied Arabic remains unchanged. Checked https://quran.com/14/37 .
overrides.duas.note.336: English mechanically calls the displayed wording a dua, but the row and the cited narration identify it specifically as the talbiyah. Urdu uses talbiyah rather than the generic label.
overrides.duas.note.342: English mechanically calls the displayed Allahu Akbar wording a dua. It is the takbir said at the Black Stone, so Urdu names it as takbir.
overrides.duas.note.371: English calls the displayed text a dua, but it is Surah al-Ikhlas. Urdu accurately refers to the displayed Quranic verses rather than mislabelling them as a dua.
overrides.duas.name.549: English says danger, but the narration, supplication and Bengali all concern affliction or calamity. Urdu names the actual occasion as calamity.
overrides.duas.note.551: English omits the Prophetic statement that the eyes follow the soul when it is taken. Bengali preserves it as part of the same cited Muslim 920 narration, so Urdu restores it.
overrides.duas.translation.561: English explicitly supplies the Children of Israel as the subject of 'certainly knew', while the supplied Arabic and Bengali retain the preceding unspecified plural. Urdu follows the supplied verse without inserting that interpretive subject.
overrides.duas.translation.568: English loosely renders sayubtiluhu as exposing magic's worthlessness. The supplied Arabic and Bengali say that Allah will nullify it; Urdu preserves that direct meaning.
overrides.duas.translation.572: English first calls da'iya Allahi the Messenger of Allah, then calls him the Caller of Allah. The supplied Arabic and Bengali consistently mean one who calls to Allah; Urdu uses that wording in both places.
overrides.duas.translation.560: Muhammad appears only in an explanatory English bracket for the second-person address ilayka. Urdu follows the supplied Arabic with the respectful direct address 'آپ' and does not insert the name into the verse.
overrides.duas.translation.567: Allah appears only in an explanatory English bracket after prostration. The supplied Arabic simply says that the magicians were cast down in prostration; Urdu preserves that verse wording without inserting the divine name.
overrides.duas.translation.570: Muhammad appears only in an explanatory English bracket before 'say'. The supplied Arabic has the direct imperative qul; Urdu renders it naturally as 'کہہ دیجیے' without inserting the name into the verse.
overrides.duas.translation.575: Muhammad appears only in an explanatory English bracket before 'say'. The supplied Arabic begins with qul; Urdu renders the direct imperative without inserting the name into the verse.
overrides.duas.translation.595: English omits the opening ala Allahi tawakkalna. The supplied Arabic, Bengali context, and Quran 7:89 all include reliance on Allah; Urdu restores that clause. Checked https://quran.com/7/89 .
overrides.duas.name.613: English calls the middle request devotion, but the supplied Arabic thabbit aqdamana and Quran 3:147 ask for firm footing or steadfastness. Urdu names steadfastness. Checked https://quran.com/3/147 .
overrides.duas.translation.619: English renders hukman as authority, while the Bengali gives wisdom and Quran 26:83 is also commonly rendered as wisdom. Urdu uses hikmat. Checked https://quran.com/ash-shuara/83 .
overrides.duas.name.642: English mentions only ease in speech, while the supplied Arabic also asks for an expanded breast and ease in the task; Bengali names both the speech impediment and ease in the task. Urdu title reflects the complete passage.
overrides.duas.name.656: English title is unrelated to the supplied verse. The Arabic and Bengali concern safety for the city and provision for its believing residents; Urdu names safety and provision.
overrides.duas.name.661: English title says protection from Hellfire, but the supplied verse fragment from Quran 10:22 concerns rescue from the immediate peril at sea, and Bengali simply names salvation. Urdu uses the broader accurate title 'rescue from distress'.
overrides.duas.translation.664: English includes the omitted opening of Quran 12:101 about sovereignty and dream interpretation, but the frozen Arabic and Bengali begin with 'Creator of the heavens and earth'. Urdu translates the supplied passage without importing absent clauses.
overrides.duas.translation.675: English continues Quran 66:11 with requests for rescue from Pharaoh, his deeds and wrongdoing people, but the supplied Arabic and Bengali stop after the request for a house in Paradise. Urdu preserves the supplied fragment only.
overrides.duas.translation.677: English omits the supplied Arabic wording 'light of my sight' while retaining only 'light of my chest'. Bengali notes both transmitted wordings; Urdu preserves both, keeping the chest wording parenthetical as supplied.
overrides.duas.note.679: English leaves the first-person narrator unnamed. Bengali and the cited Nasa'i 1300 identify him as Anas ibn Malik; Urdu restores his name and Companion honorific.
overrides.duas.translation.681: English awkwardly replaces both occurrences of ilah with Allah. The supplied Arabic and Bengali say that the addressee's deity is one deity; Urdu preserves that meaning without inserting the divine name into this field.
overrides.duas.translation.696: English omits the trial of wealth, adds senility, and does not cleanly follow the supplied Arabic ending. Bengali confirms the wealth-and-poverty clauses; Urdu follows the complete supplied Arabic and ends with laziness, sin and debt.
overrides.duas.content.715: English says Abbas returned after one day, while Bengali says after some days and the Arabic wording of Tirmidhi 3514 has ayyaman. Urdu uses 'after a few days', consistent with the parallel correction at row 14.
overrides.duas.name.716: English title adds stability in religion although the supplied dua asks for a good outcome in all affairs and rescue from disgrace and punishment. Urdu names the actual requests in the dua.
overrides.duas.translation.721: English conflates the named illnesses and renders judham as elephantiasis. The supplied Arabic asks refuge from baras, madness, judham and evil diseases; Urdu distinguishes baras and leprosy and follows the Arabic list.
overrides.duas.content.722: English gives the Companion's name as Qutb Ibn Malik; the actual report names him Qutbah ibn Malik, also reflected in Bengali. The frozen Mishkat 2405 reference is unrelated and is retained for a separate source-data audit; the report appears at Tirmidhi 3591 and Mishkat 2471. Checked https://sunnah.com/mishkat:2471 and https://sunnah.com/narrator/6494 .
overrides.duas.translation.728: English renders al-Muqaddim and al-Mu'akhkhir as the First and the Last. The supplied Arabic names the One who advances and delays; Urdu preserves those meanings.
overrides.duas.name.732: English title says after death, but the supplied Arabic and the actual supplication concern old age and the closing part of one's lifetime. Urdu names that actual period.
overrides.duas.translation.738: English is truncated and omits the contrast in the supplied Arabic. Bengali preserves it: a bad neighbour in a permanent home is especially harmful because a desert or travelling neighbour moves away. Urdu restores the full meaning.
overrides.duas.content.746: English incorrectly says the Prophet recited this after Fajr. Nasa'i 1301 has Mihjan ibn al-Adra narrating that the Prophet entered the mosque and heard another man supplicate after completing his prayer; Urdu restores that setting. Checked https://sunnah.com/nasai:1301 .
overrides.duas.name.747: English calls this specifically a request for forgiveness, but the supplied supplication invokes Allah by His greatest name and leaves the request general. Urdu uses the accurate broader title.
overrides.duas.name.748: English calls this specifically a request for forgiveness, but the supplied wording bears witness to Allah's oneness and invokes Him by His greatest name without an explicit forgiveness clause. Urdu uses the broader accurate title.
overrides.duas.translation.749: English opens with O Allah, while the supplied Arabic says Rabbi and Bengali likewise addresses my Lord. Urdu follows the actual invocation: اے میرے رب.
overrides.duas.note.750: English vaguely says a man followed Ammar. The narration is Ata ibn al-Sa'ib from his father, and it was his father who followed Ammar, asked about the supplication, and returned to the people; Urdu keeps that chain clear, consistent with row 235.
overrides.duas.content.763: English gives an unrelated generic invitation to use a powerful supplication. Abu Dawud 1522 has the Prophet take Muadh's hand, affirm his love for him, and advise him never to omit this dua after every prayer; Urdu restores the cited context. Checked https://sunnah.com/abudawud:1522 .
overrides.duas.translation.764: English renders na'iman as tranquility. The supplied Arabic and Bengali ask for an enduring blessing that never runs out; Urdu follows that meaning.
overrides.duas.translation.768: English says to turn away the enemy, but the supplied Arabic wan-surni ala aduwwi asks for help or victory against the enemy. Urdu follows the Arabic.
overrides.duas.name.770: The English title reduces this long comprehensive supplication to dignity, grace and revenge. Urdu names its broader requests for Allah's blessing, mercy, favour and support.
overrides.duas.translation.770: English omits wa sharra ma mana'ta minna, which is present in the supplied Arabic and Bengali. Urdu restores seeking refuge from the evil of what has been withheld as well as what has been given.
overrides.duas.note.770: English names only Rifa'a al-Zuraqi while Bengali names his son Ubayd. The cited chain is Ubayd ibn Rifa'a narrating from his father Rifa'a; Urdu restores both narrators and their correct honorifics. Checked https://sunnah.com/adab:699 .
overrides.duas.content.772: English and Bengali attribute the report to Anas ibn Malik, but the matching Tirmidhi 3173 report is narrated by Umar ibn al-Khattab. Urdu restores Umar's name while leaving the missing frozen reference untouched. Checked https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:3173 .
overrides.duas.group_items.772.0.content: English says whoever 'implicates' the ten verses will enter Paradise, which is not meaningful here. Tirmidhi 3173 says whoever abides by or fulfils them; Urdu says whoever acts upon them. Checked https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:3173 .
overrides.duas.translation.781: English repeats the sacrificial-slaughter mistranslation of qurbatan. The supplied Arabic and Bengali ask that the hurt become a means of nearness to Allah on the Day of Resurrection; Urdu restores that meaning, consistent with row 483. Checked https://sunnah.com/bukhari:6361 .
overrides.duas.translation.787: English is corrupted after the first two clauses and omits the supplied requests for long life and forgiveness. Urdu follows the complete Arabic and Bengali wording: increase his wealth and children, lengthen his life, and forgive him.
overrides.duas.name.789: English title says the dua is for Abu Hurayrah and his mother, but the displayed Arabic and the narration concern guidance specifically for his mother. Urdu names the actual recipient.
overrides.duas.note.793: English names Muhammad inside Abu Jahl's abusive instruction. In natural respectful Urdu, after identifying the Messenger of Allah, the same referent is expressed as آپ rather than repeating the personal name. The event wording was checked at https://sunnah.com/muslim:1794a .
overrides.duas.translation.794: The supplied Arabic and English say al-Walid ibn Uqbah, but the narrator of Muslim 1794a explicitly identifies that name as an error, and the corroborating chain in Muslim 1794c gives al-Walid ibn Utbah. Urdu uses the corrected name. Checked https://sunnah.com/muslim:1794a and https://sunnah.com/muslim:1794c .
overrides.duas.name.795: English calls this a dua against Suraqah ibn Malik. The cited narration describes the supplication when he was pursuing the Prophet during the Hijrah, so Urdu names that precise occasion without implying enduring hostility. Checked https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3911 .
overrides.duas.note.800: English and Bengali date the Battle of Ahzab to the fourth Hijri year. The stronger and majority chronology places it in Shawwal of 5 AH, while noting a reported fourth-year view; Urdu gives the stronger view. Checked https://islamweb.net/en/print.php?id=157960 .
overrides.duas.translation.810: English conflates the named illnesses by using leprosy and elephantiasis. The supplied Arabic asks refuge from baras, madness, judham and evil diseases, and Bengali distinguishes baras from leprosy; Urdu preserves the Arabic list as برص، دیوانگی، جذام اور بری بیماریاں, consistent with row 721.
overrides.duas.note.825: English says the Lord is nearest in the middle of the night and calls layughanu mere preoccupation. Tirmidhi 3579 specifies the last part of the night, while Muslim 2702 uses the restrained covering metaphor. Urdu follows both cited reports, consistent with rows 380 and 389. Checked https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:3579 and https://sunnah.com/muslim:2702a .
overrides.duas.translation.826: English narrows thamarina to dates. The supplied Arabic asks blessing for all fruits and Bengali also says fruits, so Urdu uses پھلوں.
overrides.duas.translation.828: English literally says the evil of my semen. Abu Dawud 1551 glosses this as sexual passion, and Bengali explains unlawful discharge; Urdu expresses the intended protection naturally as شرم گاہ کے شر. Checked https://sunnah.com/abudawud:1551 .
overrides.duas.note.830: English accidentally calls the benefactor responsible for thanking the benefactor. Bengali correctly assigns that duty to the person who received the benefit; Urdu restores the intended roles.
overrides.duas.translation.839: English and Bengali shift one fullness clause from the heavens and earth to what the Book counted. The supplied Arabic has fullness of what is in the heavens and earth, followed by the count recorded in the Book, then the count and fullness of all things. Urdu follows the Arabic sequence in both halves.
overrides.duas.note.840: English is badly corrupted after the opening. Bukhari 5376 tells Umar ibn Abi Salamah to mention Allah's name, eat with his right hand and eat what is nearest to him; Urdu restores the complete instruction and his closing statement. Checked https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5376 .
overrides.duas.note.847: As in row 830, English accidentally assigns gratitude to the benefactor instead of the beneficiary. Bengali preserves the correct roles, which Urdu follows.
overrides.duas.note.850: Muhammad appears only in an explanatory English bracket for the direct Quranic address. Urdu follows the verse with respectful direct imperatives and does not insert the name.
overrides.duas.translation.852: English uses singular 'I seek refuge', but the supplied Arabic na'udhu is plural. Urdu correctly says 'we seek refuge'.
overrides.duas.note.858: English and Bengali describe one goat and its jaws. Bukhari 5565 explicitly describes two horned black-and-white rams and the Prophet placing his foot on their sides; Urdu restores those details. Checked https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5565 .
overrides.duas.translation.864: English and Bengali render al-afiyah merely as security. The supplied Arabic and Tirmidhi 3514 ask for comprehensive well-being in this world and the Hereafter; Urdu uses عافیت. Checked https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:3514 .
overrides.duas.translation.866: English calls al-ghasiq a disappearing moon. Urdu follows the supplied Arabic image of the darkening or enveloping moon while retaining the row's lunar context.
overrides.duas.translation.867: English and Bengali say willingly and unwillingly, but the supplied Arabic distinguishes what was done by mistake from what was done deliberately. Urdu preserves that distinction.
overrides.duas.translation.869: English omits that Muhammad is Allah's servant, although the supplied Arabic says abduhu wa rasuluhu and Bengali includes both. Urdu restores 'His servant and Messenger'.
overrides.duas.translation.870: English and Bengali omit the second blessing phrase represented by Arabic mubarakan alayhi. Urdu preserves both blessing phrases naturally.
overrides.duas.translation.873: English omits wa bihamdika. The supplied Arabic and Bengali include praise together with glorification; Urdu restores it.
overrides.duas.name.874: English places this wording in ruku, but Bengali and the wording li-rabbi al-hamd place it in qawmah after rising from ruku. Urdu names the actual position.
overrides.duas.name.876: English again labels a qawmah supplication as being in ruku. Bengali correctly places it while standing after ruku, which Urdu follows.
overrides.duas.group_items.877.5.note: English says 'Shariq al-Hawzani and I', leaving an unidentified first-person narrator. Abu Dawud 5085 has Shariq himself visit Aisha and ask the question; Urdu restores that chain and correct honorifics. Checked https://sunnah.com/abudawud:5085 .
overrides.duas.translation.882: English renders amanataka as safety. The supplied Arabic explicitly says amanah, so Urdu uses امانت, consistent with row 321.
overrides.duas.translation.884: English begins O Allah, omits the request for mercy and renders al-Akram as Merciful. The supplied Arabic begins Rabbi, asks forgiveness and mercy, and ends al-Aziz al-Akram; Urdu follows the complete Arabic wording.
overrides.duas.name.892: English title mentions only halal provision, but the supplied supplication also asks forgiveness, support, life, righteous deeds and good character. Urdu title reflects the broader requests.
overrides.duas.translation.892: English and Bengali add high rank and explicitly halal food. The supplied Arabic instead asks Allah to raise or support the supplicant, grant life and provision, and guide to righteous deeds and character; Urdu follows the Arabic.
overrides.duas.name.897: English labels the field a dua for warriors, but Muslim 1731 presents it as the Prophet's instructions to an appointed military commander. Urdu names it as guidance to the army. Checked https://sunnah.com/muslim/32/3 .
overrides.duas.note.897: English again calls the displayed military instructions a dua and awkwardly generalizes the appointment. Muslim 1731 states that the Prophet gave this counsel when appointing a commander; Urdu preserves that setting. Checked https://sunnah.com/muslim/32/3 .
overrides.duas.translation.905: The English translation is heavily corrupted and the Bengali imports explanations. Urdu follows the supplied Arabic clauses directly: Allah feeds but is not fed, bestowed guidance and provisions, is never dispensable, clothed after nakedness, guided from error, granted sight after blindness, and favored humankind over much creation.
overrides.duas.name.909: English calls this protection from rain damage, but the supplied Arabic asks about the good and evil of the wind and Bengali says storm. Urdu names the actual windstorm context.
overrides.duas.name.910: English again calls this protection from rain damage, while supplied Arabic laqhan la aqiman and Bengali concern a rain-bearing rather than barren windstorm. Urdu names the windstorm context.
overrides.duas.name.911: English again says rain damage, while the supplied Arabic and Bengali concern what the windstorm has been commanded to bring. Urdu names the windstorm context.
overrides.duas.translation.911: English mistakenly repeats seeking refuge from evil in both clauses. The supplied Arabic and Bengali first ask for the good the wind was commanded to bring, then seek refuge from its evil; Urdu preserves that contrast.
overrides.duas.translation.912: English and Bengali omit the supplied Arabic hani'an. Urdu preserves both qualities by asking for a pleasant, beneficial downpour.
overrides.duas.translation.914: English's 'wreak havoc' overstates Arabic yanka'u laka aduwwan. Bengali and the Arabic ask that the healed servant be able to harm or wound an enemy for Allah's cause; Urdu uses the restrained idiom 'zach pahunchana'.
overrides.duas.translation.920: English misassigns the four Arabic contrasts. Supplied Arabic jiddi wa hazli wa khata'i wa amdi asks forgiveness for what was done seriously or in jest, by mistake or deliberately; Urdu follows those pairs.
overrides.duas.content.932: English calls the Prophetic heart wording 'unmindfulness'. Urdu retains the restrained covering metaphor of layughanu ala qalbi, consistent with the reviewed parallel wording in rows 380 and 389.
overrides.duas.content.936: English wrongly says the Prophet recited this after leading Fajr. The cited Nasa'i 1301 report has Mihjan ibn al-Adra narrate that the Prophet entered the mosque and heard another man supplicate after completing his prayer; Urdu restores that setting, consistent with reviewed row 746.
overrides.duas.name.937: English labels this specifically as seeking forgiveness, but the displayed invocation asks Allah generally by His greatest name and contains no forgiveness clause. Urdu uses the broader title, consistent with reviewed row 747.
overrides.duas.name.938: English labels this specifically as seeking forgiveness, but the displayed invocation bears witness to Allah's oneness and asks generally by His greatest name. Urdu uses the broader title, consistent with reviewed row 748.
overrides.duas.translation.943: English translates only Quran 14:41, although the supplied Arabic contains 14:40-41 and Bengali translates both verses. Urdu preserves the complete supplied passage without adding number labels absent from the English target field; the frozen Arabic and reference remain unchanged.
overrides.duas.translation.960: English renders al-Muqaddim and al-Mu'akhkhir as the First and Last. The supplied Arabic names the One who advances and delays; Urdu preserves those meanings, consistent with reviewed row 728.
overrides.duas.translation.981: English omits the opening reliance clause ala Allahi tawakkalna. The supplied Arabic and Bengali include it; Urdu restores the complete supplied verse, consistent with reviewed row 595.
overrides.duas.translation.994: English omits the opening of verse 9, wa qihim al-sayyi'at. The supplied Arabic and Bengali ask Allah to protect them from the consequences of evil deeds; Urdu restores that clause, consistent with reviewed row 409.
overrides.duas.translation.995: English continues with the final clause of Quran 59:10, but the supplied Arabic deliberately stops before it and row 996 stores that clause separately. Urdu translates only the supplied fragment to avoid duplicating the following row.

overrides.ruqyah_instants.translation.8: English adds refuge from the evil of everything created, but the supplied Arabic asks refuge specifically from every devil, harmful creature and evil eye. Urdu follows the supplied Arabic, consistent with Bukhari 3371.

_notes: Categories and subcategories were translated from the English WITH the Bengali (reference_bn) beside it.
Where the two disagree the Bengali was followed, because it matches what the category actually contains.
Example: category 2 is "Dua's Excellence" in English but holds Tasbeeh/Tahmid/Tahlil/Takbeer, which is dhikr - the Bengali says dhikr, so the Urdu says ذکر.
Example: category 37 is "Prophet's Dua" in English but contains the duas of Adam, Ayyub and Yunus (AS) - the Bengali plural was followed: انبیاء و رُسل.
